key_insight: Snoring sounds can be used as a non-invasive acoustic biomarker to distinguish palatal from epiglottic upper-airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnea.
clinical_relevance: If validated further, this approach could help triage or complement DISE by suggesting the likely anatomical site of obstruction from audio alone.
method: Retrospective study of 159 DISE recordings from adults with moderate, non-positional OSA
Expert reviewers labeled snoring events; only fully agreed-upon events were kept
Extracted spectral, cepstral, temporal, and harmonic features and trained SVM/MLP models with patient-independent nested cross-validation
evidence_signal: From 1,759 snoring events (1,054 palatal, 705 epiglottic), both models achieved ROC AUC 0.90 ± 0.03, with balanced accuracy of 0.83 for SVM and 0.81 for MLP.
watch_item: Results come from a retrospective, DISE-labeled dataset in a specific OSA subgroup, so broader real-world performance and generalizability still need prospective validation.
paper_title: The sound of snoring: AI-based acoustic phenotyping of upper airway obstruction in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
